BasePK: 2337923

Speech:
Before the hon. member resumes I would like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that we have been hearing interruptions ever since he started his remarks. I would point out that those making the interruptions are French speaking members who are so tender about their rights in the House of Commons. Being myself a French Canadian 1 feel ashamed to have those of my own blood making all these interruptions, and I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to enforce the rules on them so that decorum may be reestablished in the house.

You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

{"topic": "<short noun phrase>", "procedural_score": 0.0}

BasePK: 2338236

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, it is a rather strange thing when the leader of the Cre-ditiste party will say in the house in the flag debate that the design of the flag, to use his own words, "is of little concern to me". Then he went on to say, as found on page 10742 of Hansard:
However, I do not oppose the adoption of another design provided it is Canadian-
He also said:
... let us remove the maple leaf and put a beaver, or a sheaf of wheat, or indeed anything else-
No member of the Liberal party objected to that statement, and it is customary in this house in a proper debate for people to answer arguments of which they do not approve. I say, sir, that in view of the fact that the Creditistes have taken this stand it is incumbent upon us to draw this to the attention of the people of Canada, because I believe that people who are going to say they care nothing about our national flag, that they do not care what is on it-

BasePK: 2338249

Speech:
This verges almost on subversive tactics, Mr. Speaker, the destruction of things that are treasured by Canadians. I say now, Mr. Speaker, that during the course of the debate last summer and from the action of the committee I have discovered that no compromise on the issue of the flag is possible in the present House of Commons, and that is why the issue should be referred to the people. We have had this clearly demonstrated by the failure of the committee. After all its meetings the committee failed to come up with a compromise. I said earlier that I was under the impression months ago that a suitable compromise would be the addition of the maple leaf and the fleur-de-lis in prominence on the Canadian red ensign. I was wrong.

Canadian Flag

Speech:
I will answer the question. I regret that the hon. member is unable to follow an argument very closely. I said it had been my opinion several months ago that the fleur-de-lis would represent French Canada on our flag but I have found out during the course of the debate and as a result of the proceedings of the committee that I was wrong. That is why I say the people of Canada need to know the situation, because hundreds of people have written to me and friends have spoken to me who have been in favour of a compromise, and in their opinion it was always that the Canadian red ensign should be modified in order to give greater recognition to the French founders of this country.

BasePK: 2338349

Speech:
I would like to give you another fact, Mr. Speaker. The Gallup polls only measure a very small number of people but they do try to give some evidence of what the people in the country are thinking. The latest figure we have had from a Gallup poll, I believe, indicates that approximately 50 per cent of the people polled want some form of new flag; but it also indicates that 42 per cent want the present flag, and about 6 per cent have no opinion. This means, Mr. Speaker, that we are dealing with a flag for which there is no majority of support as yet, because it is a new flag, and the house is being asked to accept it. In other words, because 50 per cent of the people want a new flag, all the rest must accept it. I would suggest that when a Prime Minister wanders about this country speaking on one hand about unity and reaching out with the other hand slapping his party down into miserable conformity, to divide this country by bringing in a flag like this, those actions should be spoken of in language that everyone can understand.
Why do we want a plebiscite? First of all, I do not think there is any chance of persuading any person in this house to accept views other than those he has made up his mind on: I do not think there is any chance of making one vote's difference or change here. But it is our duty to fight on as hard
Canadian Flag
as we can to give the people a chance to speak on something that is their right, namely to decide the flag that flies over them. The fairest way now, in view of the attitude in the house, is to let the country decide; and if the decision is made in a plebiscite that will give them their right to express their will; the minority will obey the wish of the majority. I also point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that many of us have fought very hard to get here and none of us likes the burden of elections. But this government, now wracked and torn with dissension as it is, faltering in its last few months before it disintegrates, has to face up to the people one day; and when they do each member opposite will have to stand up and answer for his actions.
Those from the poor areas of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes will have to go before their farmers, who have the lowest income of any part of Canada, and say, "We have not done anything for you; but look at the beautiful white and red flag". Ask them then about your wonderful fight for this new flag, which not one of you stood up and supported. When I say "not one", I use that expression in the euphemistic sense of "very few". We want a plebiscite held.

BasePK: 2338352

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, some of the debate across the house is due to the provocative nature of my remarks. Hon. gentlemen opposite are usually quiet and mannerly and act like $1,500 a month men should act; but since they have chosen me for their target I am glad to accept their challenge. I should like to make my views clear, and my time is running out. I suggest that we hold a plebiscite to give the people the chance to decide the matter.
I do not know whether you will rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, but before you take any action in this regard, what I want to discuss now is the type of things which the committee should recommend as matters to be dealt with on a plebiscite which will make sense. We have already suggested to the house that the plebiscite should contain four choices. Obviously with the three maple leaf flag shot down in flames the proposed committee flag will have to be left as one of the choices on a plebiscite. Because of the strong emotional feelings for the red ensign, that will have to be left off. Therefore I am going to propose

Canadian Flag
at this time, as a suggestion from an individual member of the opposition and not from a party, that there is still one chance for us to come out of this matter united. I suggest we realize the strength of feeling behind the traditional, distinctive national flag we now have, but at the same time realize the strength of feeling which would be created by a brand new flag. My suggestion is that we get down to basics and realize that most people in this country are not ashamed of their past, be they English or French. We would all like to have on our flag our own symbols. If the union jack is not acceptable because it is an indication of subservience to a colonial structure, let us take off the union jack the two crosses, one white the other red; one standing for the cross of St. Louis which was flown on the ships in which Jacques Cartier landed here in 1534, and the other the cross of St. George which was the standard of John Cabot when he landed here. I know that many French Canadians do not regard John Cabot as the equal of Jacques Cartier, but that is a small consideration in the achievement of unity. I know that the Scots, the Irish, yes and the Welsh, will feel a little unhappy that their symbols have been removed. But for the sake of unity I suggest that if we had the two flags of the two founding races, the two crosses, we would have both insignia that I and my party want to see.
I think that if there was a willingness in this house to reach some sort of compromise instead of complete division, and we could get 80 to 90 per cent of the members together-and they could come together on this -if the government still wanted to fight for a maple leaf flag I am sure that not one of us would oppose the emblem of the maple leaf centred on the two crosses. Whether it was a green or red maple leaf I do not think would bother us too much. But if this flag compromise were reached, I would hope that the background would be either blue or red. I say that, because who wants to see a white flag flying over Canada? Colour is very important to us.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) had his own suggestion about a flag. He unveiled it in his counties and found wide acceptance for it. He tried it out in deep dyed ensign country and it was found acceptable there. Why would it not be acceptable to the members of parliament here?

BasePK: 2338490

Speech:
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I have learned to distinguish between sophisms and syllogisms, I have learned that with syllogisms one can argue in two ways, either by induction or by deduction. Today, my argumentation is quite simple, I proceed by induction. That is why, in the light of the figures I am going to quote, you will notice that the conclusion will be drawn automatically and that is why I shall keep on quoting those figures.
Mention has been made of newspapers. If we take for granted that about six million people take an average of five minutes a day to read what is published on the flag issue, this amounts to 140 minutes for 28 days. Six million people reading an average of 140 minutes amount to 840 million minutes, or 14 million hours.
If we consider now the news bulletins on radio and television, which take an average of ten minutes a day-it is more, but let us assume it is ten minutes. This amounts to 280 minutes in 28 days. With a minimum average of six million listeners and viewers, this amounts to 1,680 million minutes or 28 million hours.
We now have, Mr. Speaker, a grand total of 43,958,555 hours on the flag issue.

Canadian Flag
If the average salary is $3 per hour, up to now the flag debate has cost $131,875,650.

I wish my hon. friend would allow me to deliver my speech in my own way, because I am coming to those various matters. He has brought up these two points, so perhaps I should deal with them now.

In so far as the first point is concerned, it was raised in the early days of the debate and I answered that at the time. There has been no change since that time. I said then, and I repeat now, that naturally when a resolution of this kind was before the Canadian parliament the Queen, through the high commissioner in London, was informally apprised of the fact that this resolution was before parliament. Her advice was not sought. It would have been quite unconstitutional to ask for her advice on a matter which had not yet been decided upon by the Canadian parliament. If I had done that I can imagine what my right hon. friend would be saying today. He would be accusing me of dragging the crown into politics. What we did, as a matter of courtesy, was to inform the Queen of the action or the proposal that was before the Canadian parliament, and indicated to the Queen that if that proposal were accepted she would be asked to take the necessary constitutional action, as Queen. This cannot be done, of course, until parliament has declared itself.
In so far as the second question is concerned, the question of a commonwealth flag, that was not mentioned at the prime ministers' conference at all. It did not come up in any way, shape or form, nor has it come up in any commonwealth meeting since of which I am aware. I have made informal inquiries of certain commonwealth leaders as to whether it may be practicable to consider the possibility of some emblem which would be common to all states of the commonwealth. However, it is quite impracticable at the present time and may be impracticable for a long time to come because of the very nature of the states within the commonwealth. There are monarchies in the commonwealth, are monarchies that recognize the Queen of England, the Queen of Canada or the Queen of Australia. There are republics in the commonwealth. But surely, in this day and age, it is not either wrong or unusual to have emblems flying in a country which denote different forms of association of the people of that country with different international or national organizations.
I believe, therefore, it is logical and desirable to retain in this country an emblem of our association with the other members of the commonwealth. Even though it is not a commonwealth flag, it is a flag which would denote Canada's association with the commonwealth. I will try to explain later why I think the royal union jack is the most logical and best emblem for that purpose.

Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, Waterloo South is an English speaking riding. It has very strong United Empire Loyalist roots; its people are proud and hard working; it is the home of the Highland Light Infantry of Canada, a great regiment with many battle honours; it has four branches of the Canadian Legion, all of them doing extremely well; and it is proud of the red ensign. I have followed this debate with great interest and great emotion, as hon. members will understand. I have spoken to many people in Waterloo South about the flag, and their feelings regarding it. I think the people in Waterloo South recognized very early that Canada needed a new flag, a flag that would not be hyphenated, a flag that would not say "French Canada", "English Canada" or any other Canada, but only one Canada. I believe this parliament has accomplished that; we now have that flag.
The people in Waterloo South could have waited for a flag. They could have waited, because they were most reluctant to transfer their loyalty from the ensign that they love to another flag which they will learn to love. But I think it should be recognized by many of the members of this house that we could have waited. There are other members of this house who could not wait. We recognized that fact and as good Canadians we said they had real, just grievances and we were prepared to meet those grievances. I refer to the grievances of French Canada. I believe we have shown our willingness to do this. We now ask those French Canadian members of this house to recognize, much as we understood their feelings and the justice of their cause, that we have very strong and real feelings for the ensign.
We have heard them say that if another flag is necessary and there was a flag representing the world, this is the flag we should accept and honour rather than one which only recognizes our commonwealth relationships. When that day comes and that flag is ready to be accepted, a flag that represents the brotherhood of man, the universality of all people, I will be one of the first to vote for it if I am fortunate enough to be here. Mr. Speaker, I am hopeful that the parliamentary schedule will make it possible for the house to deal with the important revisions of the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act, and amendments to the Bank of Canada Act early in the new session. In the meantime I wish to make a short statement respecting the holding of shares in our chartered and savings banks.
The house will recall that on September 22 last when Bill C-123, an act to amend the insurance, trust and loan companies acts administered by the department of insurance, was introduced I mentioned that provisions similar to those limiting non-resident shareholdings in federally incorporated insurance, trust and loan companies would be contained in amendments to the bank acts which would be introduced later, and that these new provisions would also be effective as from September 23 last.
It was fortunate that the government's intention in this regard was made known at that time because I have reason to believe that if this had not been done, effective control of one of our chartered banks with facilities all across the country would by now have been acquired by non-resident interests.
In recent months there has been considerable discussion concerning possible concentrations of domestic ownership and control of Canadian banks and the ownership of bank shares by provincial governments. Traditionally, share ownership of Canadian banks has been dispersed among a great many investors
Statement on Bank Shares so that no small group of shareholders has had effective control of any of the major Canadian banks. The government feels it is desirable to ensure that this situation will continue. Accordingly there will be included in the proposed amendments to the two bank acts limitations on the number of shares of a bank that may be registered directly or indirectly for the benefit of any one resident as well as for any one non-resident shareholder. The proposed limit applicable to any individual or corporation will be 10 per cent of a bank's total outstanding shares, with special provision for temporary exemptions in the case of a newly formed bank and an exemption for any existing holdings that may be in excess of this 10 per cent.
The British North America Act clearly assigns to parliament exclusive jurisdiction over banking and the incorporation of banks. It is the intention of the government that this responsibility of parliament and of the government under the authority of parliament shall be maintained and not be eroded. Even a limited ownership of shares of a bank by another government, whether it be a foreign government or a provincial government, could place such government in a special position of power or influence in relation to that bank. Such a situation might lead to differences of opinion between this government and another government, and to confusion over who exercises authority in regard to the bank. In order to avoid this danger, the proposed amendments will provide that no shares of a chartered or savings bank may be registered in the name of any government or its agents.
If any transfers of shares of a bank are registered after this date and before the coming into force of the revised bank acts, which would have been required to be refused under the revised acts, it will be provided that such shares not have voting rights.
I should add that the government would welcome more competition in the banking field and is hopeful that private members' bills proposing the incorporation of two new banks might be dealt with expeditiously.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to what the Minister of Finance has just suggested will be the policy of the government respecting ownership of shares of chartered banks in this country. I also agree with the first part of his statement wherein he states he is hopeful that amendments will be brought before a committee of this house early in the new session dealing with a review and revision of the Bank Act. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to remedy the grievance suffered by creditors who cannot collect their just debts from federal civil servants because the crown's certificate of employment is a certificate of protection against the garnishee of wages process of the courts.

More than 300 years ago the British House of Commons cleaned up a similar injury to the public caused by members who used their parliamentary privileges to protect their employees and servants against the debt processes of the courts. On November 28, 1661 the House of Commons passed the following resolution:
This house, taking into further debate the great grievances of the people occasioned by protections,
Resolves, that all protections, and written certificates of the members of this house, be declared void in law, and be forthwith withdrawn and called in, and that none be granted for the future. . . .
-and on January 31, 1781 the house amended the standing order to make it more effectual by adding a punishment:
and if any protection or written certificate shall be granted by any member, such member shall make satisfaction to the party injured, and shall be liable to the censure of the house.
For 304 years the treasury bench has sat on this example we members of the House of Commons set them. The government should now do what we did, either adopt this bill and wipe out this class privilege or, if it intends to perpetuate it, make satisfaction to the injured creditors.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The Unemployment Insurance Act twisted the law, and it was my hon. friend's own party that did it, if what he is saying is twisting the law. But what I submit is the correct state of affairs is this: Because of the nature of the fishing industry both on the east and west coasts, and undoubtedly the inland fisheries as well, a commercial fisherman is a workman who works for wages. But also because of the nature of the industry people in the past have given him a designation which makes him neither an employee nor an employer but which puts him in some middle class. This has been the difficulty which has confronted the commercial fisherman ever since parliaments and legislatures started to enact legislation in connection with the relationship between workmen and companies. That is where the twisting of the situation came about both by parliaments and legislatures which either did not understand the full situation or did not want to understand the situation, but instead wanted to enact legislation which would put the commercial fisherman in a much poorer position vis-a-vis his relationship with other workmen.
That is all we are attempting to do-to put before the minister and the government the full details of what is a commercial fisherman, the problems with which he is confronted, and why he should be considered in the same class as other people who work for wages. Whether you can call him an employee or a workman or something similar really does not matter so long as you are interested in making the determination that a commercial fisherman is a person who works for wages, and as such should be in no different position than the minister himself, that is to say, one who pays a portion of his income, within the maximum limits set out in the bill, toward the Canada pension plan and who likewise has somebody called his employer who pays an equal amount toward the Canada pension plan.

Mr. Chairman, clause 15 deals with the maximum contribution and I just want to say a few brief words on this. I think there is a place in the Canada pension plan for an individual to make an arrangement to pay more than the 3.6 per cent if he chooses to do so. There are a number of people in Canada, particularly the self-employed and farmers, who have a very variable level of net income. Over a long period of time it may average out to about $3,000 or $4,000 net income on which they would make their contributions. Nevertheless, during such period, say a 10 year period, there could be a number of years when there would be no net income at all. These self-employed people, however, may have assets or some money from which they could make a contribution to the Canada pension plan and thus build up their potential pension benefits.
It seems to me that at the present time the maximum they can build up is 3.6 per cent of their earnings in any one year. A lot of people are going to fall short of earning a maximum potential benefit in the application of these maximum contribution clauses.
I should like to hear from the minister as to whether some consideration could be given to enabling the self-employed to contract to pay a higher level of contribution in those years when their earnings are down for any reason. If the plan is actuarially sound and they wanted to pay 5 or 5J per cent or even more of their net income, they would not be doing any disservice to others in the plan by making these larger contributions. I am more interested in evening out the contributions between those years when their net income may be very low and when the selfemployed would in fact show a loss, in which event they would be unable to contribute to the plan at all.

Canada Pension Plan

Speech:
Subclause (3) of section 26 would take care of the problem raised by the hon. member. This subclause reads in part as follows:
Where any book, record, writing or other document is seized, inspected, examined or produced in accordance with this section, the person by whom it is seized, inspected or examined or to whom it is produced or any officer of the Department of National Revenue may make or cause to be made one or more copies thereof and shall, upon request by the person from whom the original document was seized or by whom it was produced, in any case where a copy thereof has been made pursuant to this section, send a copy thereof to such person or, if no copy thereof has been made pursuant to this section, allow such person at any reasonable time to have access to the document so seized or produced, and a document purporting to be certified by the minister or a person thereunto authorized by him to be a copy made pursuant to this section is admissible in evidence and has the same probative force as the original document would have if it were proven in the ordinary way.

This is a provision which is not in the Income Tax Act and which I, personally, believe probably should be in there. It permits the Department of National Revenue to get away from the problem of seizing people's documents and holding them for an indefinite period of time. Under this provision the records which would be kept would be payroll records of the employer. We would, through the provisions of subclause (3), be able to get these documents, have them photostated, and produce the photostats of the documents rather than having to hold the original documents as evidence. I believe the problem raised by my hon. friend is dealt with effectively. We can assure him if someone wanted the records back we could use the photostat copies and return the records to the person involved.

My friend seems worried about the benefits being lost. The benefits will not be lost because we will require the province to fulfil this obligation at that particular time. If the province changes the plan subsequently to provide additional benefits or assume additional obligations, and a person then moves back into a province which is under the Canada pension plan, he would have to get two cheques on his retirement. What this plan does assure is that people who have built up benefits under this plan will get those benefits because of the requirement that before a province can get out it must provide in its plan for similar benefits.
With regard to portability and a person getting a single cheque, which my hon. friend has indicated is of concern to him, this will

be the case as between Quebec and the Canada pension plan. Presumably, and I must use the word "presumably", it would also be the case if any other province opted out. Speech:
There is provision in section 91 of the Old Age Security Act for the governor in council to make certain regulations. One of them provides for the payment of benefits to a person or an agency on behalf of anyone who is incapacitated. Clause 123 was intended to be the corollary of those requirements. The requirements respecting the incapacity of a pensioner under the Old Age Security Act are subsections (1), (2) and (3) of regulation 13. In these instances, where the director has stated that a pensioner by reason of infirmity, illness, insanity or other cause is incapable of managing his own affairs he may direct that the pension be paid to an agency or an individual on his behalf. There is also a requirement that the agency or individual receiving the money has to account for it in a form which the director may indicate.
Normally, the authorization of an agency or body capable of acting for someone who is incapacitated in these circumstances is a matter of provincial law. Lawyers will be familiar with the term "public trustee". I think all the provinces have made arrangements in this respect though I am not certain which officers act in all cases. But this is a matter for the provincial governments-it is for them to say which individual, commercial or state agencies shall be accepted.
The situation may arise where a monthly pension cheque is the only asset of someone who has to become a patient at a mental hospital. It may be that a daughter or other relative has had to look after this aged person for some time, incurring doctors' and other bills. She may be able to show by affidavit or otherwise that these debts were incurred on the patient's behalf, and the cheque may then be sent to reimburse her. In each case it is a matter of who is qualified under the provincial law to act instead of and for the benefit of the person who is incapacitated.

Speech:
I am not a member of that committee, but I understand from some of the members that much of the time that committee has sat, it has been extremely influ-

ential upon the government. In any event, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to argue that committees simply will never have any role in the parliamentary system, we might as well throw in the sponge right now. The important question, surely, is whether or not it is desirable that the committees should be allowed to meet at times when the house is not in session. If we do revise our committees structure along the lines proposed here or similar lines, if we reduce the number of members on each committee-if we do all the other things that are recommended, should we also go along with the idea that the committees meet, whenever possible, when the house is not sitting?
The hon. member for Villeneuve suggested that this was not either particularly necessary or desirable. However, would we not all agree that the pension committee did an extremely good job and had very regular attendance from its members, sitting as it did during much of January when the house was not sitting? The only difficulty was that most of the members had to give up their short recess in order to attend the meetings. The members with whom I have talked have agreed it was extremely worth while having the committee meet when the house was not in session, but they were slightly unhappy about having to give up their recess.
My understanding of the proposal is that the committee on procedure is not suggesting that we give up the regular recesses. It is still the hope that there would be a Christmas recess, Easter recess and summer recess. What the committee is proposing is that in addition to what we hope are ordinary recesses when the members get home and have time, particularly in the summer, with their families, there will be other periods of adjournment during the session when committees will meet and when members will have an opportunity to attend to constituency affairs. If it should be discovered that the work of parliament cannot be done under these circumstances, if it should be discovered that this provides, in effect, too many recesses, I would agree with many hon. members that it would be unwise to give up the Christmas, Easter and summer recesses.
However, do we have to conclude that the work of parliament cannot be done unless we have parliament sitting at all times other than at just the regular recess periods? If we implement the proposal concerning estimates -that they should be referred to the various standing committees some time in the future- and if we implement, when the appropriate standing order comes forward, the proposal

that a maximum of 20 days will be spent in committee of supply in this chamber, surely we are right there tightening up the time that parliament needs to spend on supply. Similarly, is there any reason in relation to other matters-not supply but regular government bills-that we cannot, once we get this system going, develop over a period of time certain time limits on debate on matters which have been thoroughly discussed in committee? That surely will be one of the next important steps we will take, whereby if we really make the most effective use of our committee we will perhaps be able, as we are with supply, to have generous limitations on debate when government bills come back to the house.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the motion for concurrence in this report was moved yesterday in accordance with what I thought was the general wish of the house that there would be a one day debate on the report, that one day of course to be a full day and not a Wednesday or a Friday. We proceeded throughout the day and had a rather useful and extensive debate. Near the conclusion of the debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) dealt with the report in a fairly comprehensive way and indicated the importance that the government attached to many of the recommendations in the report. He then went on to indicate that he would welcome the changes in the standing orders that would achieve the objectives set out in part of the report. He had already dealt with other things not in the report, had indicated their importance and had gone on to indicate with regard to two of the changes in the report, one having to do with the committee structure and the other having to do with the desirability of referral of estimates to committees, that they were substantial changes and that he hoped something could be done to bring forward actual standing orders that could be considered by the house and either accepted or rejected. In any event, the point I want to make is that he indicated the importance and urgency that the government attaches to this matter.
I had assumed, maybe wrongly but certainly my assumption was based on general

discussions, that it would be agreeable that after a day's debate had taken place, the matter would be left for later consideration. Since it is an interim report only and not a final report, the committee has full authority to go ahead. Because I had understood from conversations with committee members that they in their turn were willing and anxious to go ahead, I believed that the committee should refine their suggestions further, in a way that would involve the presenting of specific standing orders for consideration by the house. In any event, as was demonstrated this morning, my assumption was wrong.
In the circumstances in which we find ourselves, we are now at a stage where I think all hon. members will agree that we are seeking to bring this session to a termination and get on with the new session, and the government has indicated only a very few items of government business that have to be finished. We have in fact discussed at some length the exact procedure for terminating this session and starting the new one. In the light of that, I do not propose at the moment to enter into a discussion of the report in detail, much as I should like to do so. Rather, I should like to repeat what I said this morning by way of a point of order when this motion was first called.
I sought then to bring about some agreeable conclusion to the debate on this report, a conclusion agreeable to the main body of opinion in the house and, I hope, acceptable to all others who might not be in full agreement with what was being done. I made one or two suggestions and those suggestions did not seem to find acceptability. I do not know whether or not they were worthy of it. In any event, they did not receive acceptability in the house.
I think there is a consensus among members of the house to go on to other business and I am prepared to move that the report be referred back for further consideration. In doing so, I want to state again, as I did on the point of order earlier, the concern of the government to make progress with any procedures or changes in the procedures that will improve the ability of the house to handle its business. I think that wish is shared by all hon. members. Since this is a committee matter and as I am not a member of the committee, it is not proper for me to say what the committee will do. But I have in mind their past history, the number of reports they have already made, this being the fifteenth, some of which have been very good and have resulted in action
Procedure Committee Report being taken. I know from conversations I have had that the committee members are anxious to proceed.

The group consistently earning less than $600 per year and the group of self-employed individuals earning less than $800 per year consists, in the main, of farmers and fishermen. I have some figures in relation to the earnings of fishermen in certain provinces and I hope that all hon. members representing constituencies in Newfoundland, Quebec, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick will listen carefully to these figures, which refer to the average annual value of landed fish, per fisherman, in the years 1960 to 1962.
In Newfoundland, which has some 18,800 commercial fishermen, the average landed value of fish per fisherman was $850. From that figure they will have to deduct their expenses, so it is certain that the average fisherman in Newfoundland will not qualify for benefits under this plan.
The average landed value of fish per fisherman in Quebec in the period 1960 to 1962 was $875. In Prince Edward Island the average per fisherman was $1,345. Again from my general knowledge of fishing I would state that half of that value would go to expenses, so these fishermen will not qualify. In New Brunswick the average landed value of fish per fisherman was $1,400. It is certain that the majority of fishermen in that province will not benefit under this plan. Surely the majority of small farmers in Quebec and in the eastern provinces will not benefit in any way, or in a very small way, from the Canada pension plan.

Another shortcoming of the Canada pension plan is that for many years those people who earn the most money will receive the greatest bonus, while those who earn the least will receive the smallest bonus. For example, a self-employed person who retires in 1981, after the plan has been in operation for 15 years, and who contributes on the basis of average earnings of $5,000 a year, would receive a windfall to the extent of $20,000. That individual may well have earned $10,000 to $20,000 per year. Provided he earned at least $5,000 per year he would receive a windfall of $20,000. On the other hand, a person whose income was only half that, or $2,500, would be less able to provide for his retirement but would receive a bonus of only $10,000. Under the provisions of this plan the relationship of benefits to earnings progresses downward until it reaches the minimum, at which time the bonus becomes almost negligible.
Furthermore the discrepancy between what a person with a high income level will receive and what a person with a low income will receive is aggravated in the future by the provision for acceleration. For example an individual who receives the maximum, or $100 per month, if the consumer price index went up over a ten year period at 2 per cent per year, would receive $2 per month more. On the other hand, an individual whose pension was $20 per month would receive an increase of only 60 cents per month. After ten years the difference in increases between the pension of $104 per month and that of $20 per month would become not $82, but $100, so it can readily be seen that the escalation provisions of the bill will aggravate the discrepancy.

For example, a man with an income of $20,000 a year will pay only $43.45 per year toward the plan. This is because he is in the 45 per cent tax bracket and he is therefore able to deduct 45 per cent of the cost of his contribution. On the other hand, a person who has an income or gross salary of only $5,000 a year will pay the full contribution of $79 toward the plan.

The objectives of our Canadian dairy policy are twofold. The policy is designed to provide

dairy farmers operating economic units with an adequate income, while at the same time assuring the Canadian consumer a constant supply of the highest quality dairy products at stable prices which will ensure optimum consumption.
Because of its geography and climate Canada is a relatively high cost dairy producing country. Except for certain specialty products, such as mature Cheddar cheese, we cannot hope to be a significant competitor on world markets with dairy products from countries with lower production costs arising from milder climates. Because of our climatic disadvantages in dairy production it would be unrealistic to provide a level of support on all milk produced that could result in surplus production and a possible return to a costly accumulation of stocks.
A further objective of a national dairy policy must therefore be to maintain a reasonable balance between production and disappearance of milk and dairy products, account being taken of export possibilities and of imports. To this end it is proposed that government supports will apply only to domestic utilization as related to a base period. The policy will also recognize the interest of Canada's trading partners in the Canadian market for dairy products, and will permit imports to share in future market growth.
Last year Canada imported a record 17 million pounds of cheese. This was more than balanced by Canada's growing cheese exports of over 30 million pounds.

I am informed that first class mail coming into Canada is sorted at the post office, and items which might conceivably contain commercial importations are turned over to the customs officers. If customs, on examining the outside of the item, decide no further examination is required, it is stamped and returned to the Post Office Department. Speech:
The matter brought before the committee by the hon. member for Oxford is one that deserves an answer in greater detail than was given by the President of the Privy Council. The President of the Privy Council is thoroughly acquainted with the problem of the civil service of Canada. For 25 years he has represented a constituency in which there are many civil servants. I say he must have found that in the last year or so there has been a feeling of fear and frustration in the civil service.
The morale of the civil service is greatly subject to a feeling that all is not well, and this is due to the uncertainty of the utterances of the Prime Minister and other ministers in connection with the subject of bilingualism. No one has any argument to raise as to the necessity for the preservation of the principle of bilingualism in every regard, but surely those in the civil service today have the right to know what is the attitude of the government, and who in the government speaks with authority.
We have had a number of trumpets played by representatives of the government, all more or less with an uncertain sound. Is it intended that all civil servants desiring promotion shall have a full knowledge of both languages? The minister has stated that the Prime Minister made a speech somewhere, but speeches made outside the House of Commons do not answer the legitimate desire of civil servants to know what the situation is.
Is it the intention of the government that promotions are to be denied to civil servants, who for years have been giving of their best, because they are not bilingual? I mention

civil servants in Ottawa, but what of civil servants in other parts of the country? What are the rules that are applied to them? I know something of the civil service. My father was a federal civil servant for 25 years, and I know at first hand something of the difficulties of those who serve, and also of that spirit of dedication that has characterized Canada's civil servants throughout the years.
Certainly in the last two years there has been expressed by many of those who have been 10, 15 or 20 years in the service a feeling of trepidation, of uncertainty. I feel the minister should give a fuller answer than the concise but uncertain one he has just given to the committee. The suggestion by the hon. member for Oxford that a committee of the house should be set up to examine this problem fully is one which deserves the support of hon. members on all sides. I recall one of the committees presided over before I came into the house by Mr. Pouliot, now a distinguished member of the other place, and the benefits which followed the discussions and hearings of that committee.
I should like to ask the minister to let the civil servants know frankly what the situation is. It is no answer to say that the Prime Minister spoke somewhere; that is merely passing off a serious question, one which is exorcising the hearts and souls of civil servants everywhere. What is to be the attitude? What determination, if any, has been made, first as to bilingualism in Ottawa and, second, as it affects civil servants in other parts of the country? Knowing the capacity of the President of the Privy Council for giving lucid and complete information I would ask him to be a little more generous in providing the committee with information than he was a few moments ago. Let him not leave this matter in a state of uncertainty. Uncertainty breeds a lessening of morale. Fear denies that high rate of efficiency which our civil service enjoys.
I ask the minister, one who is sincerely interested in the civil service, to rise now and give an explanation to the house which will dissipate the fears being expressed in the civil service, and will give to those who serve a degree of certainly which at the moment they do not possess.

At that time it was stated that the government did not wish this action to be retroactive and provision was made in the section quoted by my hon. friend to give the Department of National Revenue the right to make refunds to particular taxpayers in order to alleviate any retroactive effect of the legislation. The date, December 31, 1964, which is the only thing that is being changed by this particular amendment, was put in in order to arrive at some finality with regard to the determination of when these refunds should be made.
Since that time there have been representations to the government indicating that there are some contracts in Canada which were entered into prior to June 13, 1963 and which could not possibly be completed by December 31, 1964. The position of the purchaser is fully protected by the fact that he has a fixed price contract. However, the position of the vendor or person who has to perform the service is not protected and therefore he is caught in a squeeze. He must absorb against his business operations any losses arising because of the application of the sales tax on construction materials.
I think it is very important that this item be passed in order that these contractors, who entered into these fixed price contracts in good faith before the enactment of the legislation, may continue to receive the same sort of treatment they have received to date under the legislation as originally enacted. If this were long delayed it would put the particular contractors in a very dangerous position financially in some instances and I commend the vote to the house as an alleviating item to allow us to deal with these contractors in the future in the way we have previously dealt with them.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Spadina asked a question arising out of articles that appeared in the Toronto newspapers about a Chinese named Ngar Mye Lau, also known as Jack Mar, and I promised a full statement early this week. These are the facts. Early last September the Royal Canadian Mounted Police received information and had occasion to investigate the circumstances under which this man, known as Jack Mar, obtained a Canadian passport. He had been in Canada for some nine years prior to that date. As a result of these investigations the facts were laid before the Assistant Crown Attorney for the county of York on September 9, 1964, and he authorized the prosecution of the man in question under section 58 (1) of the Criminal Code for obtaining a passport by giving false information and he instructed that the man be charged on that same day. An information was laid on September 9 and a summons was served on that day.
Inquiries of the Ministry
On the following day, September 10, Jack Mar visited the immigration office in Toronto to say that he wished to make an adjustment statement. He did not say that he had been charged with an offence, and he did not ask for assistance of any kind. The immigration officials assumed he was but one of the many Chinese who were visiting the office to indicate a desire to make adjustment statements. Consequently his name was put on the lengthy list and no priority was given to it.
On September 11, he appeared in court pursuant to the charge and the case was finally heard on October 15. He was convicted of making a false statement resulting in his obtaining a passport, and he was fined $1,000 or four months in jail. An appeal was taken to the Court of Appeal. In the meantime he had paid the fine.
I should like to make it clear to interested members and the public generally that at no time, so far as I can discover, did Jack Mar or his counsel seek any assistance or advice from immigration officials in pleading his case before the courts on the grounds of the so-called Chinese amnesty program. In any event, after his conviction the Parliamentary Secretary to my colleague the Minister of Justice, on December 16 last, in reply to question No. 2,161 which had been placed on the order paper, stated that Ngar Mye Lau "did not qualify for the amnesty because it applied only to illegalities related to illegal entry and did not apply to subsequent illegalities not related thereto".
When this man applied for the passport he had been in Canada for nine years and had had a period of approximately three years in which to adjust his status and to become a resident in good standing. Mr. Chairman, this resolution is some sort of a draft for the bill which will be introduced here eventually.
I thought it would contain other provisions than the one setting the retirement age of senators at 75, giving present incumbents the choice of retaining their seat even if they are past the age of retirement or to retire with full benefits as far as pension and other benefits are concerned if they have reached the age of 75.

This would enable us to have a younger Senate who would understand better present day problems, not only with regard to one part of the country but concerning Canada as a whole. A little while ago the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was telling us that he and his government had introduced a bill for that purpose a few years ago when there were 208 Conservative members in the House of Commons and that the Liberals had then voted against this measure as well as the New Democratic Party members, the CCF at that time.
The Liberal government is now introducing such a bill and the opposition does not know whether to vote for it or against it.
This is a clear evidence of the lack of seriousness of the two political parties who succeeded each other at the head of the government of Canada since Confederation. It is nevertheless the Canadian people who pay for the nonsense indulged in on either side with regard to the Senate, the senators and the setting of a retirement age.
A little later, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that himself and his party were in favour of the abolition of the Senate purely and simply.
Considering the present constitution and structure of the Senate, I believe that its abolition would be in no way prejudicial to the Canadian people but, on the contrary,
Retirement Age jor Senators would be greatly profitable because we waste a lot of time while waiting for the decisions to be made in the other place.
For instance, we would support Senate reforms which would make for a more representative Senate. For instance, agriculture should be represented by one or more senators coming from the farming community. We would need representatives of the unions to speak for the working classes in Canada; representatives of professional groups such as teachers, lawyers, physicians, engineers, economists and industrialists. There should also be in the Senate someone to speak for our young people, someone who could defend the interests of that large and important segment of our society. There should also be representatives of women's associations, not necessarily representatives of Liberal, Conservative or Creditiste women's associations, but simply representatives of women's associations in Canada. Also, in the religious community, the various religions existing in Canada should have respective spokesmen in the Senate. For some years now many Canadians have been increasingly concerned about the degree of foreign ownership in our country. What we must consider are the other aspects of foreign capital, the long term effects on our ability to manage and decide our own affairs, the kind of capital we are importing, where and how it is being invested and whether any regulation is desirable or even possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have not too much to say, particularly as I observe that other Members of the party of the hon. Member who moved the motion are prepared to speak, thus preserving the life of this unfortunate Government for some period beyond today, giving them a further chance for repentance. In view of the fact that the amendment as moved indicates the desire of the hon. Member who moved it, and presumably his party, that it should act as an expression of their view that the Senate should be abolished, I find myself in the position of being unable to support the amendment which has been proposed.
I am not going to go into the merits of the other place, which has been the subject of a very exhaustive and excellent debate on the part of those who have preceded me. My own personal experience of the Senate, which is limited to serving on various joint committees with hon. Senators, has been that they bring a faculty of deliberation, understanding
Retirement Age for Senators and experience which has been very useful indeed. In addition to these investigative and examining facilities which they have developed through a number of committees which they have established, plus the continuity of service of those in that Chamber, they have the legislative faculties provided them under the constitution.
It may be there are valid criticisms to be made of the procedure of their appointment. I think we recognize that even our own Chamber is not free from criticism, the Government having moved recently to bring in some very substantial changes to our rules. I think that this admission that there is room for improvement does not necessarily mean that at this time we should be prepared to accept the view that the Senate should be completely abolished.
I suggest that there is a reasonable element of virtue in almost any political organization or group. Even my hon. friends sitting to the left in the N.D.P.-even though there may be some who doubt this- given sufficient time in this House and the opportunity to listen to the words of wisdom which fall from those who sit in this part of the Chamber may yet at some time in the future come to a state of grace. I have my doubts, but I give them the benefit of the doubt and I say that it may happen.
I only wish I could say the same of those on the Government side, but I am afraid that in this case it is not at all likely. Even though they are frequently drenched with oratorical fertilizer, I fail to see that this strikes any spark of life in hon. Members sitting opposite. So I draw this exception.
Coming back to the motion and descending from the Government to the Senate, I think that with the changes in appointment that time will bring, and with the more specific role which experience has indicated is essential, there is no reason at all why that august body cannot continue to make very useful and reasonable contributions to the public life of this country. Having in mind that the amendment proposed is one which will kill the bill, its being an indication of the views of the party which has moved it, I feel that I cannot support this amendment.

The legal rate of 6 per cent is being maintained on the surface. If you borrow money from a bank and sign a note you will be charged 6 per cent, the legal rate, but for the past couple of years the banks have been employing certain back door methods by which they can make more interest on their money.
One method, of course, is the elimination of the overdraft practice and the requirement that notes be given for money borrowed from the chartered banks. The way this has worked out is that in most cases the banks now require a depositor to keep a credit balance in his account by virtue of notes. By doing this they are in almost every case charging interest on money which is in a current account and for which they allow no interest, so there is a double interest feature involved.
Then there is also a more recent innovation in most banks in that if perchance there is an overdraft, even in a current account, they pay the cheque but they charge 50 cents as a handling fee. On a very small overdraft a handling charge of 50 cents can mean quite a large amount of interest. I think it is well known in the banking field that this is happening, and in fact the banks are having difficulty in maintaining the interest rate of

6 per cent which is what they are allowed to charge legally. I would have hoped that some way could have been found to remove these back door methods of charging interest.
There is one more matter to which I wish to refer, the competition faced by the chartered banks from the so-called near-banks that are growing in numbers in Canada. I referred to the question of mortgage loans and the matter of interest rates, both of which are affecting the chartered banks. They are having difficulty in meeting the competition from other corporations which are permitted to charge greater interest rates. While the provision with regard to chartered banks dealing in mortgages will increase the interest rate in some cases, nothing has been done with regard to the over-all interest rate so as to permit our chartered banks to compete with these near-banks which are causing them so much difficulty.
I see it is almost ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and we are anxious to have this bill go to the committee and to have the matters I have raised and a good many others studied very thoroughly. Therefore I will say no more at this time in the hope that the bill can be given second reading immediately.

The French Secretary of State for Scientific, Atomic and Space Affairs, Mr. Yvon Bourges, and the Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Honourable Mitchell Sharp, have concluded today a series of talks on matters pertaining to a sale of uranium by Canada to France. I made it clear during the discussions that in accordance with the firm policy of the Canadian Government, the proposed sale of uranium could be only for peaceful purposes. Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to contribute to this debate after the learned discussion which has preceded my intervention but I would like to say a word or two at this time. Following the very skilful speech of the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the speeches of other hon. Members perhaps I should not take part, but on the other hand I feel I would like to make a few general observations with respect to the nature of the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
The hon. Member for Edmonton West was very much concerned with the method under which committees are to be set up to study the estimates. He felt there was a danger in restriction of discussion on the floor of the chamber, but I was very much impressed when the Prime Minister pointed out that actually debating time will be longer in the House of Commons than hitherto. We will be sitting longer hours. We will be sitting through the dinner recess and at other times, and a longer period of time will be available to each Member of the House. I was impressed with the Prime Minister's argument and I feel that when committees are set up all the estimates will be given more attention than they have received in the past.
One cannot argue that no change is justified. It is commonly understood, from one
House of Commons Procedures end of the country to another, that our rules are antiquated and outdated. I felt a measure of personal satisfaction when the Prime Minister introduced this resolution to reform the rules of parliament in order to make them suited to conditions in 1965 because these rules, with few, small, rather insignificant changes, have existed ever since Confederation. The business that goes through parliament today is so tremendous, compared with that done in parliament in years long past, that surely it is high time the rules, after consideration in this chamber, be amended on the suggestion of the Prime Minister, who has assumed the responsibility.
I am wholeheartedly in support of what has been proposed. Changes may have to be made later on, and changes may be made before the resolution is passed in final form. I do not know that; but at any rate a great attempt is being made to create a lasting reform of the rules so that the business conducted in the House will be done in an efficient, modernized way, tailored to meet the problems that arise for parliament in the times in which we live.
I would not think of setting myself up as an expert comparable with others who have taken part in this debate. Accordingly my remarks are general in nature, but I feel I am speaking for my constituents when I say that long needed reform is at last being brought about by the leader of my party, and I am very happy to support this measure. I do not wish to be partisan and I will certainly try not to be but, as I said, I have a lot of personal satisfaction and some measure of pride in the fact that our leader took it upon himself to introduce this measure.
The opening words of the resolution are very meaningful:

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, we do not like the amendment in itself and we feel it is out of order. Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules, 1943 edition, page 139, states that an amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.
With all due respect to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and others who have gone into this question of a permanent Speaker, surely it is apparent that these changed rules, if passed, can be effective whether the Speaker is permanent or not. The basis of the motion that is put forward is that it would be a better protection and provide some safeguards, but that is not really pertinent to the resolution before us.
One of the most regrettable things that has happened in this debate was the initiation of the discussion of a permanent Speakership, and in a sense I believe that the Chair, early on in the debate, may have been at fault in allowing that particular part of the discussion to go so far. It is apparent, especially since personalities have been injected, that this is a potentially embarrassing situation. It points up the irrelevancy of the kind of discussion about these matters, because we have had mention of three particular persons.
We have something that is fairly concrete and clear before us, and discussion of a permanent Speaker has absolutely nothing to do with it. I not only suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you rule the amendment out of order but that you take it upon yourself, perhaps in consultation with your officials, to tighten up the whole discussion on whether we should have a permanent Speaker. The feelings of certain people are involved, and if you do not do this we are going to have a pretty bitter and disgraceful discussion in the House, because a great many of us are highly opinionated and prejudiced in this regard, particularly with regard to some of the personalities suggested.

BasePK: 2371679

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will have a self-imposed time allocation of not more than 15 minutes and perhaps less. I want to deal with one particular aspect of the debate.
There seems to be a recurring theme in the speeches of members of the Conservative and Liberal parties about the good old days when there were two parties in the House, that the House was designed for two parties and that it would be wonderful if this were the way it could operate. It has been a very long time since that has been the case in Canada. In fact the last election which returned two parties to this House was that of 1917, and possibly it was only one and a half parties at that time because half of the Liberal party was in the Union Government of the day.
I think we should be reminded periodically that following 1917 there was the election of 1921 which returned 117 Liberals, 59 Conservatives, 64 Progressives, 3 Labour and 1 Independent. The 1925 election returned 101 Liberals, 116 Conservatives, 24 Progressives, 2 Labour and 2 Independents.
In 1926 we had large third and fourth groups, that election having returned 116 Liberals, 91 Conservatives, 11 United Farmers of Alberta, 13 Progressives, 9 Liberal-Progressives, 3 Labour and 2 Independents. In 1930 there were 137 Conservatives, 88 Liberals, 10 United Farmers, 2 Progressives, 3 Liberal-Progressives, 2 Labour, 1 Independent Labour and 2 Independents. In 1935 there were 171 Liberals and 39 Conservatives.
Indeed, for the benefit of the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), I would point out that in the Parliaments of 1935 and 1940 there were only 39 Conservative Members. The hon. Member talked about setting a high limit on what should be considered a party. I point out that his party shrunk to 39 on two occasions and to 41 on another. It could happen again next year. In any event in 1935 the figures were 171 Liberals, 39 Conservatives, 17 Social Credit, 7 C.C.F., 5 Independent Liberals, 2 Liberal-Progressives, 1 Independent Conservative, 1 Reconstruction, 1 Independent and 1 U.F.O. In the Parliament of 1940 there were 184 Liberals, 39 Conservatives, 10 Social Credit representatives, 8 members of the C.C.F. party and a number of others called Liberal Progressives, Independent Liberals, Independent Conservatives, Independent, and so on.

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Throughout the years ever since the election of 1921 there have been third or fourth parties or a large number of independent members. So it is a long time since we have had a straight two-party system in Canada and I suggest the situation will not change in a hurry.
Some Members have put forward the view that changes in the rules would encourage the multiplication of parties. That is nonsense. It has nothing to do with the rules of this House but concerns rather dissatisfaction with the policies followed by existing parties. The fact that the Social Credit party elected a great many Members to this House from Quebec in 1962 and 1963 had nothing whatever to do with rules of the House of Commons. Electors will vote for the candidates who appeal to them regardless of what our rules are here.
Yesterday the hon. Member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) referred to the question of the definition of parties. We have made some progress in this direction during the last two years in this House, particularly in 1963. The hon. lady mentioned the practice in the National Assembly of France. I am partial to this idea though I do not think we can realize it quickly in Canada. Nevertheless it needs further exploration and study. It is useless to carry on the pretence that political parties do not exist, as is done in many of our rules and, indeed, in the Elections Act itself. Parties do exist. Most of us would not be here were it not for the support of the political parties of which we are Members. People would not vote for us as independents. The role played by the parties in elections and in the operation of Parliament should receive further recognition. I realize this presents difficulties but we have made a beginning by recognizing the existence of more than two parties.
For a long time in Canada, indeed, for nearly 45 years, there have been more than two parties in the House of Commons. Taking into account the fact that parties have been recognized by the rules of the House since 1963, I believe that many of the arguments put forward during this debate by representatives of the Official Opposition particularly fall to the ground. We should recognize now that there is every possibility that as a result of any future election there will be other parties represented in this House beside the Official Opposition.

As everyone knows, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the two Canadas were the colonies which formed the dominion in the first instance.

When the question of what to call this confederation arose, it was known to be a contentious one. Those responsible wanted to evolve a name which would give a new breath of understanding to anyone who referred to this union. It was no longer to be called Canada only. We recall that in those days Canada was a limited area. In very general terms it comprised the watershed of the St. Lawrence River system. The other colonies were never known as Canada. Indeed, they had no connection with Canada. Canada at that time was just as foreign to them as Bermuda or the West Indies. I find it strange that an argument can be advanced that this in some way is likely to
2264	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures infringe on the rights and privileges of backbenchers. I say it seems strange, having in mind the fact that I have not heard anyone complaining in this House that the arrangements made for the debate on the Budget and the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, each limited in extent, constitute an infringement of the rights and privileges of backbenchers.
We know that even if all the provisions contained in the new standing order 15 were used it would be impossible for a Government to limit a debate to less than one day on the resolution, in the case of a bill, two days for second reading, two days in committee after second reading and one day plus an overtime period of four hours on third reading. I would also draw to the attention of the House the fact that in addition to these six days there is also a one day debate which can be demanded on the motion to impose these rules. Therefore, every time this Standing Order 15A is used, provision will be made for an amount of time to be spent on one single piece of legislation at least equal to that which is available for discussion of the Speech from the Throne, a discussion which is, I suggest, of far greater magnitude inasmuch as it embraces the whole of the Government's legislative program for the session.
Indeed, even more time will be allowed taking into account the extra hours which will be available each day. At present the debate on the Budget is limited to six sitting days of about five hours each day. In other words it is limited to about 30 hours. This debate on the Budget involves the whole of the Government's fiscal policy for the year. Yet even should the Minister use every one of the provisions of this standing order he cannot provide for less time on a single piece of legislation than is now available to backbenchers to deal with the Government's whole fiscal policy for the year.
I cannot, therefore, accept the argument that this proposed standing order is in any way an infringement or a curtailment of the right of backbenchers to participate in debates. What it does is this. It provides that we shall move on from one piece of legislation to another within reasonable time limits. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the most effective form of closure we have witnessed in this House is the abuse of these open-ended debates which prevents us moving from one piece of legislation to another.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two brief observations. I think most of us have thick enough skins that we can bear the impact of the guillotine without too much difficulty. In reply to what has been said by the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of Transport, I would point out that a close examination of the new committees indicates that there have been some completely new innovations. For example, we are to have
June 11, 1965	COMMONS
a Committee on Human Rights and a Committee on Crown Corporations. Certainly these were at no time included within the phraseology of committees which were capable of being established under the previous Standing Order.
Something has been said to the effect that we should be patient and wait for the years to go by. It may be because of my great age, Mr. Chairman, but from my experience in the seven or so years I have been here it seems to me that the period of gestation between the time someone gets a gleam in his eye and the 10 or 15 or 20 years it apparently takes to implement the idea in the form of legislation is just too many years for me to have to wait, and I hope there are other Members of the Committee who feel the same way.
I recall that when I came back from war service I tried to rehabilitate myself in a knowledge of the law. In the City of Edmonton I went through the library and looked at the federal and provincial statutes. Then the librarian showed me row after row of volumes with page after page of Orders in Council passed during the course of the war. It would have taken many men studying day and night for years to absorb the knowledge and authority contained in those Orders in Council.
Two or three years ago I had the privilege of serving as Chairman of a small committee which inquired into the Emergency Measures Organization and the War Measures legislation. At that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare was a member of the committee. She asked the Clerk of the Privy Council, I believe, to bring before the Committee some of the Orders in Council dealing with this particular phase and we were told that it would take a truck to bring them all to the committee room.
This is the danger that we face at this time. It is like the old Roman emperor who, in order to comply with custom which compelled him to publish the laws, had them engraved on tablets of stone and then hung so high that no one could read them.

western hemisphere and Australasia, and enables peoples of many tongues and races to meet together with a common loyalty to common democratic objectives.
