I am glad to have the opportunity to take part in a debate on a subject which so seriously affects farmers in this area. The general situation is one which brings to mind the droughts on the prairies in the thirties. I must say I wish there were more Members from the West here today to show a sympathetic interest in the problems of some of the eastern provinces. I congratulate the hon. Member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) on the measures he was prepared to support.
Without question we are facing a serious emergency. A number of suggestions have been made from all quarters of the House as to what might be done. Measures to deal with the situation, both short-term and long-term, will have to be brought forward. I know that the Minister himself has been much concerned about the situation. But at this point I should like to go on record as saying a few things concerning the lack of action on the part of the Ontario provincial Department of Agriculture. The ARDA program was put on the books while the party opposite was in power. I heard a great deal about what was going to be done for the Ottawa Valley. They were very proud of it. What, in fact, was done before this Government took office? There was not a single ARDA project approved for
June 23, 1965

any one of the counties affected by this drought. Schemes were submitted to Toronto and they died within the provincial Department of Agriculture. The Province of Ontario has taken a narrow and restricted view of ARDA projects. They have related them to watersheds; without a watershed there can be no project. In the counties affected by this drought there are no community pastures. There are no deep wells, no public assistance arrangements for farmers.
In the thirties the drought in the West was followed by measures of great importance in reaching a long term solution of farmers' difficulties-for example, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under the constitutional arrangements which govern this country, the ARDA program was set up in such a way that grants were to be made by the federal Government. We have put a lot of new life into this program. I am proud of the enthusiasm the Minister has shown and the report he has submitted to this House. His addresses on the subject of rural poverty constitute a memorable series of speeches which I believe should be studied by scientists and sociologists across Canada.
The projects which have to go forward under ARDA arise at local municipal level and go to the provincial level. And it is there we find the dead hand; it is there we find the hand that kills, the hand that shows no initiative and no interest in a long term solution to the problems facing Eastern Ontario agriculture. The province is showing an interest in supporting a rain making project. The hon. Member for Acadia had something to say about projects of this kind. I do not know whether it works or not. Like my hon. friend from Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) I do not claim to be a farmer; but I am very much concerned about the farming communities I have the honour to represent in this House. I do know that unless some imagination is shown by the provincial authorities in the Province of Ontario, unless some interest is taken, unless they quit dragging their heels, we shall continue to suffer, in the absence of long term remedial measures. Those counties will suffer in the future as they are suffering now. The federal authorities are alert. They are concerned. Well, the loophole applies in a case where an oil or gas right can be acquired by a joint exploration corporation, but its cost can be divided by its parent corporations. A joint exploration corporation is a special kind of company defined in section 83 (a), (d) and (e), which was passed in 1962. It is a company whose principal business is the production or marketing of petroleum products or natural gas, or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas, or mining or exploring for minerals. Such a company must not have more than ten shareholders and those may be companies that are in the oil, gas or mining business. These shareholder companies provide the joint exploration company with the funds to carry out the exploration. The joint exploration company renounces its right to deduct the exploration expenses it has incurred and each of its shareholder companies acquires the right to deduct its share of these expenses.
It has become apparent that the joint exploration rules can be used as a loophole if an oil company wishes to dispose of its oil and gas properties and not bring the proceeds into income as required by section 83(a). Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief statement which I am sure will be of interest to the Members of the House. As the House is aware, the automotive plan is designed to achieve a substantial expansion in production and employment in Canada and to promote improved efficiency in the automotive industries. Under the plan production in Canada will increase by several hundred million dollars annually and employment in the industry will grow accordingly. In this regard, during the year in which the previous automotive plan was in effect employment in the automotive industries increased by nearly 10,000 workers. Under the current plan the motor vehicle manufacturers and many parts manufacturers have already announced major expansion plans.
Organized labour and the automobile and automobile parts industries have welcomed the plan as a bold and constructive measure which is in the national interest. A major economic expansion of this nature, however, is bound to result in certain transitional adjustments for some workers and firms. In such cases there may be a temporary lay-off of workers while the company re-equips. There will be instances where firms will find it necessary to expand or re-equip their facilities to produce in greater volume and in the most efficient manner.
While such adjustments will take place in the context of very substantial growth in the industry, the Government believes that assistance should be provided to those who may be affected by the adjustment process in order to ease possible interim adverse effects. As a result the Government proposes to implement a program of transitional adjustment assistance for workers and firms in the automotive products industries. My colleague the Minister of Labour immediately following will be outlining the measures which the Government proposes to implement for workers in this industry. I would like to outline the program of adjustment assistance for firms.
The automotive plan offers new opportunities to Canadian automotive parts manufacturers for expanded production, rationalization of output and reduced costs. If Canadian parts makers are to take advantage of the plan, they must be increasingly competitive and flexible in their operations. In some instances they will be asked by their customers to make new products or to manufacture existing components on an expanded scale and more efficiently. As a result many Canadian parts makers will have to engage in substantial re-equipment and expansion programs to take advantage of the opportunities provided by the plan. In addition, increased working capital will be required in order to operate at expanded levels.
The Government wishes to ensure that every automotive products manufacturer who is energetic and shows initiative will have the opportunity to participate in the plan and is not prevented from doing so by an inability to acquire sufficient capital to accomplish
2908	COMMONS
Assistance to Auto Workers these objectives. As a result the Government is proposing to make loans available to those automotive products producers who have a reasonable prospect of profitable operation but who otherwise would be prevented from doing so through lack of financing. These loans will be made for the purpose of acquisition, construction, installation, modernization, development, conversion, or expansion of land, building, equipment, facilities or machinery and for use as working capital. They will carry an interest rate of 6 per cent and would be repayable over not more than 20 years for land and buildings and 10 years for other purposes.
A special fund will be set up for the purpose of making these loans, and the administration of this program will be the responsibility of an adjustment assistance board which is being set up specifically for this purpose. The Industrial Development Bank will be cooperating with the board and will be responsible for the day to day administration of the loans which are made under the program. Firms manufacturing the automotive products covered by the automotive plan will be eligible for the loans, except for companies which manufacture automobiles or firms affiliated with automobile manufactures.
The Government feels that this transitional assistance program for firms in the automotive products industry will make a real contribution to assisting firms, especially the smaller ones, to adjust to and take advantage of the many opportunities for expansion and efficiency provided by the automotive plan.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it would save the time of the House if my colleague the Minister of Labour could be heard on the complementary labour aspects of this program before general comments are offered.

We are proposing a third criterion which provides for the designation of areas in which employment has declined persistently over a period of years. This situation may be associated with underemployment, which in general means employment for less than normal full time, or employment in an unproductive and low-paying job. Sir, in the international field we are endeavouring at all times to be in agreement. The speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, is right to the point and the program outlined for the first session of the twenty seventh par-
January 25, 1966

The Address-Mr. Matte liament could help, through the work of all its members, to maintain the growth of our beautiful Canada for the greater good of all Canadians. In addition, it will bring a ray of hope to the needy through the war on poverty already started under a Liberal government, and the speech from the throne confirms this fact.
This brings me to deal first with the economic poverty to be found within certain classes in this country; second, with the duty of government and all individuals to cope, first of all, with this serious problem; third, what has been done by the new Liberal government; and fourth, what it proposes to do in this state of war.
Although some define poverty as a purely relative fact, depending on the place and the era, to me it is the state of those who are deprived of what they need to live and to play a citizen's role in society.
Most Canadians will agree that no citizen in this country should be, through outside causes, deprived from the benefits of modern civilization. It is our social responsibility to give everybody an opportunity to enjoy a certain degree of comfort.
A great philosopher, reflecting on poverty, has concluded that a modicum of welfare is required to fulfil properly one's religious and, consequently, one's civic duties.
Although all citizens must be considered equal in the eyes of the law, a poor person's shortcomings are always more excusable. A minimum of welfare will make a man a better citizen or simply a true Canadian.
The report on rural poverty in four regions prepared and published for ARDA by the Canadian welfare council in Ottawa should give us food for thought. The discoveries made in these four countries are true, to a varying degree, of almost all the rural and urban regions of the country.
I should like to give you a summary of these conditions as seen by community leaders and by the poor families whose conception of poverty is entirely different.
The former see poverty in its overall aspect, that is, its causes and effects; in other words, they grasp the concept better. The latter define it rather in terms of their own situation and that of their neighbour.
The definition given by community leaders generally bears a close resemblance to the reasons set forth during the case survey. Here are, in order of importance, the common factors most often included by those community leaders in such a definition:

Economic poverty: lack of personal income, too heavy family responsibilities, uneconomic land or farm, chronic unemployment, jobs that do not pay enough or are hard to get.
Personal or family deficiencies: inadequate schooling of children and parents, illness, poor adaptation, irresponsibility, alcoholism, lack of social participation, slums, dire poverty, debts, mentally deficient children and parents, anxiety concerning the future, little opportunity for betterment, unfulfilled desire to improve, laziness, a single trade, old age.
Social deficiencies: unemployment, insufficient school and sanitary equipment, lack of recreational organizations (especially for the young), lack of social cohesion.
The concept of poverty in the family stresses above all the difficulties it experiences: "We are not earning enough to make ends meet", "It's tough going", "We don't know what we will eat to-morrow". Elsewhere, frustrated ambition is more obvious: "We can't give our children any education", "We can't live like others do". The lack of essentials is illustrated in the two following definitions:	"To be poor is to wash your
clothes without soap" and "It is not to have any newspaper with which to light the stove."
Certain moral causes of poverty are expressed as follows: "He is poor because he is too lazy to work." "If So-and-So is poor, it is because he drinks too much; he often goes to the hotel". And then inadequacy steps in to explain poverty; for some "Poverty is lack of education" or "It is lack of intelligence."
Well, that is poverty. And that is what we find too often when we visit our ridings and when our electors pay us a visit.
According to the report from which I have just quoted, it was found that out of 63 families visited, 40 did not earn $50 per week. There were also too many poor families among our agricultural classes. After having made surveys, experts came to the conclusion that a family must earn at least $3,000 per year to be able to survive. According to the 1961 census, 23 per cent of Canadian families did not earn that amount. That is why it seems illogical to set at $2,000 a year the basic deduction for a family.
Poverty can easily prevent an individual from being a good citizen.
Therefore, a tremendous responsibility lies with our governments which must strive for the good of every citizen and particularly of those who are most in need.

I draw attention to the fact that the C.P.R. is flouting the intent as well as the provisions of both of these pieces of legislation. It is denying to its employees consultation with regard to the effect of the Canada Pension Plan on their private pension rights, and it is also denying the benefits which that plan was intended to provide. Likewise, with respect to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code it is quarreling over every little detail it possibly can. This can only lead to a very serious situation on the C.P.R., and I feel that parliament cannot sit idly by while this sort of thing goes on.
I do not pretend to be a prophet or the son of a prophet, but I see certain things as almost sure to happen in this country if a firm stand is not taken. The Canadian Pacific Railway, because it wants to get out of the passenger service business on its railway lines, has taken this attitude. On the other hand, that same organization, with respect to its Canadian Pacific Airlines, is endeavouring to get more air routes and more opportunities to make money in that field of transportation.

I was about to say that the situation has changed but I think there were one or two interjections which would spoil that follow-up on my part. However, Mr. Chairman, because the case against the C.P.R. has been made so fully and has been documented so well, it is not necessary for me to

February 14, 1966
Supply-Transport
spend much time elaborating on that case. I do think, however, that at some point this discussion about the C.P.R. should result in a clear statement to the government as to what ought to be done.
We have to face the fact that transportation is one of those services that the public must have, and when you are concerned with a public service, in the long run it just is not realistic to expect that that service will be provided by an organization whose main interest is in the making of private profit. So long as there was huge profit to be made out of transporting people by rail, so long as there was huge profit to be made out of transporting heavy produce such as wheat, by rail, the C.P.R. as a private organization was pleased to engage in that kind of business. Mind you, it was given the tremendous start that has been documented several times during the course of this debate. I have in mind the huge grants of money and of land that were made to it back in 1880, together with the additional grants of land and money, and other benefits given to it at the expense of the public over the years.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, pointed out this afternoon that these grants run to the order of $100 million in money and over $400 million in land. I suppose there is no way of estimating what has been given in terms of oil and mineral rights, and all the other ways in which the C.P.R. has been allowed to make huge profits. I suppose there is no way of calculating what this company has received in terms of taxes it has not had to pay, at all levels of government.
One of my first experiences in public life was to be a member of the council of the city of Winnipeg. I remember our concern back in those days with the fact that the city fathers of the last century, in attempting to persuade the C.P.R. to come to Winnipeg, had guaranteed that its property in the city would be free of municipal taxes forever. Forever is a long while, and after a time it becomes very costly.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, all kinds of benefits were given to the C.P.R. in return for which it contracted to run a railroad, to run it efficiently, to provide rail service for Canada; and again the word "forever" was in that contract. But now that there is no longer profit to be made out of passenger rail service it has become quite clear that the C.P.R. is doing everything that it can to get

out of that operation. Members in all parties on both sides of the chamber have recounted again and again the way in which trains like the "Dominion" have been discontinued, the way in which service has been made unattractive, the way in which the C.P.R. is literally saying to its customers, "We don't want your business any more."
The hon. member for Red Deer made it pretty clear earlier this evening that the C.P.R. is getting itself into a position to unload at least its passenger service, and perhaps even some of its heavy freight service, onto the government of this country.
Instead of our just repeating these charges, instead of our just recounting this indictment against the C.P.R. over and over again, we should lay down a basic principle, and I think the basic principle which the government should accept and should use is this: It should say to the C.P.R. that either it must provide the railway services that the country needs, the services that it is under contract to provide, and charge any losses on those railway services against the profits of its other operations, or it should turn the whole of its operations over to the government of this country to be run as a public enterprise.

On May 15, 1963, Doctor M. R. MacCharles stated at a convention of the Canadian Medical Association, that excessive smoking was the main cause of lung cancer and that this disease was incurable.

The committee made up of 17 doctors, including cancer specialists, unanimously agreed that the situation had reached such alarming proportions that a wide publicity campaign should be launched among the public.
In January 1964, Dr. Luther Terry, a well known American physician, published a report which had been prepared by a committee of experts and stated that there was a direct link between smoking, on the one hand, and lung diseases, respiratory ailments and heart troubles, on the other. The report further said that cigarette smoking was such a serious health hazard that it was the duty of the American government to take appropriate steps in that connection.
According to statistics, Mr. Speaker, each day, 450 boys and girls ranging from 11 to 17 years of age start smoking. We all know that when a child develops that habit, it cannot do without smoking after two years.
In 1963, lung cancer made 2,500 victims in Canada and that figure is increasing at a fantastic rate from year to year.
While medical science is waging a lost battle to save those lives, the tobacco companies spend millions of dollars a year to increase their sales among adults and to entice a new generation into acquiring the smoking habit.
Although over $150 million are spent yearly for publicity purposes in North America, a very meagre sum indeed is spent in Canada to protect the public against that danger.
If the situation continues, according to a Canadian Medical Association report, cigarettes will be responsible for the premature death of nearly 100,000 children now attending Canadian institutions.
No one wants to deprive anyone else of smoking pleasure, providing he is aware of the risk involved but when the risk is hidden as in the case of cigarettes, persons should be warned by positive measures as in the case of certain drugs labelled with the word "poison". As various international discussions will be taking place over the next two or three weeks regarding the very serious food situation facing India, and as it is most important that India should know as soon as possible what supplies she can count on, I should like to inform the house in general terms of the plans of the Canadian government in this matter.
Although the Indian government is making strenuous efforts to improve the situation, there can be no doubt, as the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organization has emphasized, that without large amounts of assistance from other countries food shortages in many areas of India would reach famine proportions. Fortunately, several governments are already taking steps to help. In particular, the government of the United States of America is providing massive support.
For our part we announced some time ago that out of the 1965-66 appropriations Canada would make available to India a total of $25 million worth of food, all of which is exepect-ed to be shipped before the end of this month.
I am glad to be able to announce now that during the coming fiscal year the government plans to make available a substantially larger amount than last year. Most of this food aid will be in wheat, which India so badly needs. I expect shipment to take place after the beginning of the new crop year this July. We shall be working out the precise details in our further consultations with the Indian government and with the other governments concerned. I am satisfied that we shall be able to provide this substantial help to India and at the same time meet all our commercial orders. The fact that we can do so is a tribute to the hard work of our western farmers and the high productivity of our agricultural industry.
The situation in India requires a concerted international effort. I would hope that not only the food producing countries will help but also the many other countries which are capable of assisting with shipping, port handling equipment, fertilizers and other effective forms of aid.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, can be depended upon to make a contribution which will compare well with that of any other country.

March 8, 1968

not a department, but a health branch which came successively under the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Department of Immigration and the Department of Commerce and Industry.
Only in 1919 and at the request of the Canadian Medical Association did the department become the Department of Public Health.
In 1929, the Pensions and Civil Re-establishment Division had become less important and a Pensions and National Health Division was created. Later, following the introduction of social security programs such as old age pensions and family allowances, related in a way to para-medical problems, the Department of National Health and Welfare was set up in 1944.
Since then, Mr. Chairman, other extensive programs were added to those already administered by the department, such as hospital insurance and several national health grants. Very soon the department will also be responsible for drawing up and implementing the national medicare program and the Canada assistance plan, not to mention the Canada pension plan which is already operative.
For those reasons, the Department of National Health and Welfare should be divided into two distinct units, so that we could reorganize the whole administrative framework. When you consider also the tremendous expenditures this department expects to make to carry out its future programs, I do not think there is any other way than the one I have just mentioned. First, this would make it possible to do away with administrative routine which, when it becomes too heavy, tends to bog down and thereby ceases to advance.
Then, this would give the departments more leeway for adequate planning to provide them with greater administrative flexibility and to justify the old saying: to govern is to foresee.
We have long been bogged down in an administrative stagnation where new ideas, lest they result in small mistakes and failures, have been completely set aside, at the expense of normal progress.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the bill and to introduce a motion which I think will give the house an opportunity to discuss what I think is a matter of great importance involving a very basic principle in matters of this kind. Before doing so I want to say a couple of words about the bill itself. I want to ask the sponsor, when he is winding up the debate and before we vote on the bill, which I presume will not be too long from now, to deal with some of the questions in the minds of some of the members of the house.
I hope that the sponsor of the bill will explain to us the necessity of a stock split when there are 40 million shares in the treasury unissued. The only reason we have heard from him is that the value of the shares is rising dramatically and therefore it is desirable to split them again. However, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the shares of a great many responsible companies stand at a much higher value than do those of the company now under consideration. The explanation for the split does not seem to be reasonable or not sufficiently reasonable to convince us of the merits of the split.
We do not really want to hold the bill up in any way. We want to pass it and let it go on to the committee so that all the details that are in our minds can be examined and all the questions can be answered. We want to expedite the passage of this measure.
One of the first speakers this afternoon raised what I think is the key issue in the bill, that is, that companies of this nature should not be privately owned. That is our judgment and perhaps we may be wrong. It seems to me, however, that this is a type of company which should be publicly owned and should not be left to ownership by oil companies as at present. We are not in favour of public ownership in all circumstances but certainly any company that is dealing with a natural resource of this type ought to be, in our opinion, under public ownership. We have had good experience of public ownership in Canada with operations such as the
Private Bills
Sarnia plant, Canadian National Railways, and particularly with Ontario Hydro, a publicly owned corporation which produces electricity at the lowest cost I believe in North America, the next lowest cost producer being the publicly owned Tennessee Valley Authority.
It seems to me that at some stage in our history we shall have to take a serious look at the whole business of pipe lines. All the experts say that before many years pass pipe lines will be an important method of transporting goods. We shall not only be transporting oil through the pipe lines but we shall be transporting wheat and a great many commodities, even consumer goods. Many things will be transported through pipe lines. It seems to me that pipe lines are of such vital importance to the coming Canadian economy that the interests of the public would be served much better if they were placed under public ownership.

I do not have to rise on behalf of any particular member of the privy council in this house. The only submission I have made to you this evening is on the basis that a prima facie case of privilege exists, and there has been no debate whatsoever in respect of the merits of the fundamental question of privilege raised which has to be decided by the house and, with great deference, sir, only by the house.
I am rising this evening at the first opportunity because the matter has not been placed before Your Honour previously. On this question of privilege, I should like to draw Your Honour's attention to the words used by the Minister of Justice this afternoon when he suggested to you, sir, and this house that the conduct of the former prime minister of this country should be made the subject of a royal commission inquiry.
I submit, sir, that that is an entirely distinct and separate question of privilege which has arisen as a result of the proceedings this afternoon, and not as a result of any proceedings during the minister's estimates or anything he may have said outside the house; indeed, it is additional. The minister has simply dug himself in deeper by his remarks this afternoon. I say, sir, that he cannot hide behind such wholesale smears, slanders, and allegations without fulfilling the obligation he has to make known the full facts. He has that duty and that responsibility. He must make his charges, having gone as far as he was allowed to go this afternoon in this house and outside it. He is assumed, sir, by the public as well as by the members of this house, to be in possession of the facts and to be making charges based on substance. He must, therefore, state to the members of the house what

March 10, 1966
Question of Privilege
those charges are. If he does not do that, sir, then he is under an obligation by our procedures to resign. That is the position in which he is.
Public life would be impossible, if a minister in full possession of his ministerial authority were able to make this kind of a charge about members of this house past and present, about privy councillors and about a former Prime Minister of this country without being required to substantiate and prove them. He must name names, and he must reveal the full circumstances. No more serious charges have been made by a minister in this country.
According to the press and the radio, the minister has involved, without naming them, members of the previous government, the Leader of the Opposition, privy councillors, and I think a woman whom he says was formerly involved in espionage in East Germany. He has stated there was a report on the matter on the files of the R.C.M.P., although he has not seen that report. He has stated that the case was a bona fide security case, although he has not said it very well. He has made the charge that the former Prime Minister did not deal in a proper manner with that case. How does he know, if he has not seen the file?
He has made these charges after his estimates were passed and at a time when he knew the former Prime Minister was absent from this city. The minister's conduct constitutes a deplorable dereliction of his high office and a dastardly attack on the former Prime Minister, a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council, and every member of the former Conservative government, some of whom are still sitting in this house and who are Privy Councillors.
I submit, to you, sir, and to the house, that this must be dealt with by parliament and must be dealt with by parliament immediately, because the shabby, sordid and underhanded action which it constitutes is one which must not be allowed to be interrupted by any other order of business. The minister now must back up in this house what he said to the press outside this house, and back up in this house the charges he made against the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon.
The Prime Minister of this country is not free from responsibility. A public action of this kind by a member of the cabinet must represent the considered determination of the government. The Prime Minister and the

government must accept the minister's action or repudiate it. The minister acted following a meeting of the cabinet.
The whole government is involved in a course which has been reprehensible. It is a course of action which has been cowardly, and it is a course of action which has been lacking in the most elementary sense of justice or responsibility. I hear members over there make remarks concerning past proceedings of this house with regard to myself when I brought certain charges.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make which I hope will answer all possible questions in relation to this matter.
March 17, 1966

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company By Bill No. S-2 the National Capital Commission together with Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are endeavouring to implement the terms of an agreement made between them for the relocation of railways in the Ottawa area, dated October 17, 1963, which provides for the incorporation of a terminal railway company to consolidate and carry out rail terminal operations in the Ottawa area. This agreement was made not at the instigation of the railways but as a step in implementing the National Capital railway relocation plan.
I believe I can summarize in the interest of expedition. The bill was before the other place in 1965 when representations were made by those objecting to the wording, and again this session, the trucking companies objected to certain words which indicated that the railways might be taking over trucking in the Ottawa area. The bill has now been amended to make sure that the railway companies will only operate the normal pick-up and delivery services. There is an arrangement whereby both railway companies will share in the buildings and in the operation costs on a 50-50 basis.
A further objection was raised by railway employees who would be required to transfer to the new terminal railway company. This issue has been satisfactorily negotiated between the companies and the employees concerned so I believe I can now assure the house that all matters dealt with in the bill meet with the approval of all those who are concerned.

the second reading of Bill No. C-6, to provide for the length of sessions of parliament.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-6 was originally prepared and introduced in the last parliament at a time when there was a great deal of discussion about the need for reform of the proceedings and rules of this house. It was never debated in the twenty sixth parliament because it was not reached in private members' hour.
This is a bill to provide for the length of sessions of parliament. Since the first introduction of this bill, a special committee on procedure and organization has made numerous reports as a result of which the rules of the house have been improved and amended in many ways. I personally believe, however, that a great deal of further improvement could be brought to pass if parliament were to plan its sessions and the House of Commons were to plan its sittings, and to fix the normal times of such sittings.
Hon. members may be of the opinion that it is better to look first of all at the forest and then at the trees. I submit if the size of the forest is first determined, then the number and location of the trees can be better determined.
In recognition of the fact that parliament must sit much longer than formerly, to deal with the increasingly complex and numerous matters of public interest, and that this places a great deal of strain on the staff of parliament; in recognition of the fact that ministers of the crown have departmental duties, and all members have constituency duties which must be attended to in periods free of parliamentary duties, I have caused this bill to be re-introduced in this parliament.

I feel that if this bill, or an analogous bill, were enacted, most of the necessary routine work of parliament such as estimates, supply and minor amendments to existing legislation could be programmed for a first mandatory session in each year, and that most legislation bringing in innovations could be given first reading in the mandatory session but could be programmed for the permissive session later in the year.
I submit that this would bring order in the conduct of our business where there is now chaos. This would prevent the use of estimates and interim supply in the annual game of fox and goose played between the house leaders, a game in which they try to outfum-ble each other. This would stop the kind of emotional brinkmanship which creates the atmosphere that even brings down a government, all too unreasonably sometimes to be in the interests of the country.
In clauses 2 and 3 the bill provides for a mandatory session that commences the last Thursday of January and could continue to the second Thursday of September each year. This is the first session of the year, the mandatory session. However, the House of Commons would not normally sit beyond the last Friday of June. The Senate could continue to sit, if it so desires, to finish its business without the pressure that it has now of having to rush in order to meet a House of Commons deadline. The Senate must rise, however, some time before the second Thursday of September, whereupon the session would end. Hon. members should keep clearly in mind, as I am speaking now, the distinction between the session of parliament and the sitting of the House of Commons.
If necessary, and I believe it usually would be, there would be a fall session in which the house would finish sitting on the second Friday of December, at the latest. The Senate could continue to sit until the last Thursday of January in the new year.
Clause 4 of the bill provides for an adjustment of the sittings in an election year, and also for emergency sittings.
Clause 5 provides for a day's debate in the house on the necessity of emergency sittings, if 50 members give notice that they do not consider the call to be one of urgent public importance. This is designed to be preventive and to discourage sittings that are not really necessary and in the public interest. It is also designed to concentrate opposition criticism to one day, rather than have such criticism continue through the sittings.

Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that because the number of judges is too small in the district of Quebec, great prejudice is done to our taxpayers, and I would call the minister's attention to that point.
I am also of the opinion that the minister should study the advisability of lightening the docket, in order to help our people. In my opinion, he should appoint three new judges in the region of Quebec, which would greatly help to solve our problems.
Mr. Chairman, it has too often been said in this house that the political appointment of our judges in the superior courts or courts of appeal was questionable. As a member of the bar, I wish to protest against that tendency to let the people think that the political appointment of judges is not a good thing.
In my humble opinion, and by experience, when judges are appointed to the superior court or to the court of appeal, in short, to any court, they retain, I am happy to say, that feeling of impartiality about the ordinary man. Just because a man is appointed by a Liberal government or a Conservative government or any other, it does not mean that he does not assume his responsibilities when he becomes a judge.
I once heard a member of the house say that the method of appointing judges should be changed, because the present method is unreliable. I challenge that position and more especially, I protest against leaving the public with the impression that the appointment of a new judge is often unsatisfactory.
I think our governments appoint judges mainly because of the appointee's experience and legal knowledge. I also believe that in addition to that knowledge, a judge must equally be aware of the problems facing our taxpayers. He must have been in touch with the people and, in my opinion, a former member of parliament and government member surely has greater competence, because ir. addition to his awareness of the people's problems, he knows the problems of the parties involved, which would prove useful to him when called upon to administer justice.
I am not suggesting that the government should not intervene when certain judges behave in a manner derogatory to their

profession or their status. But nevertheless, I do want to point out that if we were always to select judges outside the political field, our appointments would not necessarily be excellent, because besides being a theorician, a judge must also be a practitioner and know at first hand the problems of the people.
I also wish to point out to the minister that he might consider the possibility of changing the method of removing a judge from office.
At the present time, the act provides that, to dismiss a judge, a petition has to be approved unanimously by both houses, that is, the House of Commons and the Senate. Now, such a procedure is extremely difficult and complicated. I do not think it has been used very often in the political history of our country. As a matter of fact, if I am not mistaken, it was only used once.
Therefore, I would ask the minister to consider the possibility of amending the removal procedure, because the government is sometimes faced with a grave problem when a judge repeatedly commits acts that are not in keeping with his functions. In such a case, the government must submit a petition to both houses, in order to dismiss the judge. I should like to see the act amended so that the bar of a province could present to the governor in council a petition, signed by the majority of its members, for the removal of a judge who had committed acts not in keeping with his functions and so that the governor in council could be empowered to deal with such a petition.
I would like it to be possible for the governor in council to be called upon, once a serious inquiry has been made with the Bar of each province, to issue an order in council to remove the judge concerned from office.
Mr. Chairman, that resolution is well looked upon and will be welcomed by the Bar of the province of Quebec. I would like the minister to take into account my remarks about the appointment of judges to our various courts.

Industrial Relations Act done in respect of labour-management relations in both of our great national railways.
